questions.q: Why does social engineering remain effective even when technical security controls are strong?
options: It targets a person's trust, curiosity, or fear directly, which firewalls and encryption don't defend against
It always requires breaking through encryption first
It only works against outdated operating systems
Modern firewalls have no effect on any attack, technical or social
questions.explain: Social engineering routes around technical controls entirely by manipulating the human component of a system, which doesn't run patchable software.

questions.q: What is the key difference between phishing and spear phishing?
options: Phishing is sent broadly to many recipients; spear phishing is researched and targeted at one person or small group
Phishing only happens by phone, while spear phishing only happens by email
Spear phishing never includes a malicious link
They are the same technique with two different names
questions.explain: Phishing is a volume strategy; spear phishing trades volume for personalized research aimed at a specific, higher-value target.

questions.q: What defines pretexting as a social engineering technique?
options: Building a fabricated scenario or false identity to manipulate a target into divulging information or taking an action
Sending the exact same email to every employee in a company
Leaving a labeled USB drive in a public area
Exploiting a software vulnerability to gain remote access
questions.explain: Pretexting works by giving the target a plausible, often urgent, reason to break a rule they'd normally follow.

questions.q: What makes baiting an effective social engineering technique?
options: It offers something enticing, like a labeled USB drive, and relies on curiosity or desire to trigger a compromise
It requires no action at all from the target
It only works against security professionals
It is a purely technical exploit with no human element
questions.explain: Baiting dangles something a target wants; the compromise happens the moment they take it, such as plugging in a found USB drive.

questions.q: A caller claims to be a traveling VP who urgently needs a password reset over the phone, with no identity verification. What makes this pretexting attempt likely to succeed?
options: The fabricated authority and manufactured urgency both pressure the target to skip normal verification steps
Because VPs are never real targets of social engineering
Because phone calls cannot be used for social engineering
Because pretexting always requires a physical USB device
questions.explain: The claimed authority (a VP) and the urgency (traveling, locked out, time-sensitive) work together to discourage the help desk from following verification procedures.
